utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. This is Monday, September 22nd, 2008, and I would like to welcome everyone here. I welcome the accused, the Defence, Mr. Scott and his colleagues, and everyone helping us, notably the interpreters. So before giving the floor to Ms. Alaburic who has a question to raise, I would like to read a short oral decision in line with what I said yesterday. Oral decision requesting the Prlic Defence to submit a new list of witnesses to the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber notes that after the time count provided by the registrar on the 19th of September, 2008, the Defence of Mr. Prlic has used so far 57 hours and six minutes for in chief in direct -- and redirect of its witnesses out of 95 [Realtime transcript read in error "94"] hours which were allocated by the Trial Chamber in the first place. On March 31st, 2008, the Prlic Defence team submitted a list of witnesses it intended to call in this case. Given the amount of time used so far, the Trial Chamber is thus asking the Prlic Defence team to provide it with an updated witness list. In this new list there should be an indication of the time the Prlic Defence team intends to allocate for the examination-in-chief and redirect for each witness. On line 22 of page 1 there is a small error. It's not 94 hours but 95 hours that were allocated in the first place. So this is the short oral -- my short oral decision and I would like to also give the floor to our registrar who has some IC numbers before we give the floor to Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Puljic, Borislav. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00844, the list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00845, the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00846, and the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00847. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Ms. Alaburic, it's me, Your Honour. But, Your Honours, I normally try to give the Prosecution advanced noticing of any application. I apologise, I just haven't had the chance the last few minutes, but I don't think it's anything that's going to overwhelm Mr. Scott. Your Honours may recall that the Petkovic Defence has filed a motion asking for reconsideration of a decision on the 1st of September in relation to two exhibits -- or four exhibits in total, two for each of two witnesses. The Prosecution filed a response towards the end of last week and this is an application - as we have to make it, Your Honour - this is an application for leave to reply. There are just a couple of points that we do wish to pick up. The draft reply is around a thousand words. It's for practical purposes done. We would be able to file it within -- well, probably later today or in the course of tomorrow. Your Honours, we ask for leave to file such a reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Stewart. The Trial Chamber grants your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are allowed, and we always love to listen to you. Let's now bring the witness into the courtroom. Correction on the transcript, line 18, it's not Mr. Scott but Mr. Stewart. There's a small mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness -- good afternoon, sir. Could you please give me your name, surname, date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ilija Kozulj born of the 18th of May, 1940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an electrical -- technical engineer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... job at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired but I'm still somewhat active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you already testified before a court or Tribunal regarding the events that occurred in former Yugoslavia or is this the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me give you some details on what will happen, but I'm sure that Mr. Karnavas has already told you about this during the proofing session. You will be asked questions put to you by Mr. Karnavas, and he will also show you documents which are in a binder. The binder of course will be placed at your disposal, but the documents will also be shown on the screen at the same time. After this first phase, the other counsels of the other accused will cross-examine you either for cross-examination purposes or maybe for re-direct, we don't know yet, but they will be allowed to also put questions to you. The four Judges on the bench in front of you can also step in at any time to put questions to you, but they usually do this when there is a document presented. The Prosecutor on your right will also ask a round of questions for his cross-examination after all the Defence teams will have put their own questions. Then after this phase the Defence may ask you some additional questions for the redirect. All together we have scheduled four days, four hearing days. We are sitting in the afternoon this week, so we will sit from 2.15 to 7.00 this week. Please try to be very specific in your answers. If you don't understand the meaning of a question, just ask the person putting the question to you to reformulate it. You have made a solemn declaration, you have sworn to only say the truth, which means that now you are the witness of justice and you are no longer on the Defence side, if I may say so, which means that you will no longer have any contact with anyone until your hearing is over. I wanted to give you all these details. Let me also add that we have 20-minute breaks every hour and a half because we need to change our audio-tapes and video-tapes, and it also helps each and everyone here to rest because you'll see that it is quite strenuous, it's -- this exercise is quite strenuous. Answering questions is strenuous both for the person putting the question and the person answering the question. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Kozulj.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me first start by going through your background, and I'll just start by leading you a little bit. As I understand it, you have a degree in electrical engineering; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please tell us when did you receive that degree?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: In January 1964 was when I graduated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it shortly thereafter you began working in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the PTT; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what does PTT stand for, just for the record?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: PTT is an enterprise, usually public enterprise, that provides services that have to do with postal services, telephone, and telegraph. Before you had the postal services and then telephone and telegraph services separate, but now it's all under one umbrella and it's called communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could you please tell us for how long you worked for PTT in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I worked about 13 years in the PTT or 14 years. I moved to the UNIS enterprise in 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we speak about UNIS, could you please tell us when you left PTT by that point at what level had you reached within this public enterprise, what level of the organization?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: When I left the PTT, I was head of the technical service, I was something like a technical director of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that at some point after 13 years with PTT you switched over to UNIS. Could you please tell us a little bit about this particular enterprise. Is it public or is it socially owned? And a little bit about what UNIS is all about.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: At the time, UNIS was a social enterprise, a large social enterprise, with headquarters in Sarajevo. It had about 100 factories and about 50.000 employees. The reason why I moved to UNIS was that UNIS at that time signed an agreement on business and technical cooperation with the Ericsson company from Sweden, and it was necessary to build a factory and develop a company that would be making telecommunications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, first, what year are we speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. 1978, and if you can please tell us, in light of this new contract with Ericsson, to what extent were you involved in this particular project?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I personally did not take part in the signing of the agreement, but when I was asked to go to UNIS and when I agreed to do that and to work at that position and to take responsibility for the implementation of these complex tasks, I was given an introduction and I was given the contract to review. And I was told, Well, this is what we signed and now you can see what you need to do. At that time, UNIS as a group didn't have telecommunications experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And specifically in just a few words, could you please tell us what exactly you did based on this contract that you were asked to basically review and implement.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: In order to build a factory, you needed to secure about $5 million US. At that time we didn't have those funds and we had to create an investment project and ask the banks for funds. That was one activity. The second activity was to put together the staff who would be working there. The third activity was to create technical specifications that would be built at the factory so that they could be used by the PTT branch in Mostar, so that they could use it. So this was a very demanding aspect of the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're speaking of taking it from the contract or from the concept all the way to its total realization where the factory's working; is that what we're speaking of?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And to what extent were you specifically involved? At what level were you in this enterprise?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: First I was the director of the company that was being established, and later I became the director of the company itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at some point as I understand it you moved to Sarajevo; is that correct -- or you were also employed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I worked in Mostar. My first assignment was to take a number of UNIS enterprises and put them together as one company after this factory was built, to create a sort of synergy, so I had to create or draft a project how to do this job, how to bring all these companies under one umbrella. After that I became the director of this larger company with headquarters in Mostar. After that, I was appointed a member of the business board of -- or governing board of the entire UNIS company, and I was in charge of the companies that were producing electronic and telecommunications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I am pausing because the translators are having a little bit of a difficulty keeping up with you, so I'm going to ask you to slow down a little bit. Now, if I can ask you, where were you when -- where did the war find you, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I happened to be between Mostar and Sarajevo. I had a temporary apartment in Sarajevo and I was still performing the duties of the member of the managing board of UNIS, but I was actually working and receiving my salary from another UNIS company that was located in Ljubljana. Most of the factory from my group happened to be in Mostar so that was the reason why I went to Mostar quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. As I understand it -- because we'll go through the documents but we've seen your name last week in one of the documents. At some point you were appointed to the special-purpose council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could please describe to us the events in Mostar, particularly as it related to UNIS, your factory, but also in general prior to you being selected to serve on the special-purpose council.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: After the democratic elections and the possibility to set up a new authority in the best possible way, tensions began, wartime activities began in Croatia. I happened to be on a business trip in Sweden as a matter of fact, and on the way back -- actually, while I was still in Sweden we heard the news on CNN that reservists and forces of the Yugoslav People's Army had come to Mostar. Of course I came to Mostar. I managed to get to Mostar without any major difficulties, but the situation in Mostar at the time was such that forces of the Yugoslav People's Army and the reservists occupied or came to certain military facilities and simply moved around the town more and more. The situation was fairly dangerous. UNIS's factories in Mostar were immediately next to the JNA barracks in Mostar so that the entrance to the UNIS factory was practically under the supervision of the military forces of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was that on the east side or the west side?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: This was on the east side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And to what extent, if any, were these factories affected as a result of the war or the activities that took place thereafter? We know that -- we've heard testimony that there was fighting, that the east side of Mostar fell. But with regard to the UNIS factories, to what extent were they damaged, if any?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, we immediately saw that the situation was difficult. There were discussions about saving the equipment and the material that we had and moving it to a safer area. Some from the several factories did that, each one of them did something but not to a sufficient degree. I must say that Mostar was very isolated at that time. Mostar had only one, conditionally speaking, free exit from town which was controlled by shelling from Serb positions. All the other roads out of Mostar were blocked. So in these conditions the special-purpose council was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And to your understanding, if you could just briefly tell us, what did you think at the time the special-purpose council was all about? Why did it come into existence and what was its aims and purposes?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: At the time we felt it was our responsibility and we also were willing to help to defend ourselves from aggression in some way. Of course younger people were willing and accepted to bear arms, but us older people were more useful in other jobs and I think the special-purpose council's role was to help in these defence situations more from the aspect of logistics and resolving problems as far as the civilian range of activities in defence was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that point in time, were you a member of a political party, and specifically, were you a member of HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you were more associated with the previous system, given that you had worked for a public enterprise? And I believe there's a particular word that they use for folks like yourself who were associated with that system at high levels.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was a member of the communist party, I can put it that way. It's more easily understood. But before the democratic changes I actually didn't wish to take my chance there. I did not join the HDZ, and even now I think that the HDZ is a movement of the Croatian people and that it's still not the right time for party divisions or options.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But fair to say at the time you were -- you would have been considered what they call - and I don't mean to disrespect you - as a "komunjara," a communist, that would be the term; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Yes, I did belong to that group that was referred to as "komunjara".

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we know from the documents that we will see that at some point you became a minister in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That would have been I believe sometime in 1993. Up until the point you became a minister of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, did you formally participate in any official capacity, that is, in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna either at the municipal level or any other level?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: No, I was just a member of the special-purpose council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if you could please tell us, throughout this period, that is all the way up until the point of time you became a minister of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, in general if you could describe to us the sorts of activities that you were involved in.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: At the time I worked as best as I could in the special-purpose council, and then at the point in time when the telecommunications facility in Mostar was destroyed I helped people to resolve some of their questions, to deal with it. And as they kept banding together and strengthening their organization, I was pulling back. I must admit that I was appointed member of the board of governors of the PTT public company when that was founded. So that was also one of my roles, and one of the important assignments was to prepare projects for the rebuilding of post offices and telecommunications in those buildings, that was the main activity. I was also helping the UNIS organizations to deal with things, to find their feet, to do something to keep their personnel and preserve the equipment as much as they could. These were my main activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And before we go into those activities in more detail, let's just continue on very briefly generally about your background. When you became a minister of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, what was your -- what were your tasks then and what -- how long did you serve in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I remained in that post until I got transferred to Sarajevo to the new post, and my tasks were now much broader than they were because in addition to the post of telecommunications I was now in charge also of other infrastructure, such as roads, road traffic, railways and railway traffic, air traffic, and river traffic, and also some technical aspects of radio and television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One of the important things in the proceedings is trying to get the dates and periods. So to the extent possible, if you could help us out. You said up until the time you moved to Sarajevo. When did you go to Sarajevo, month, year?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say now, but I think it was in 1995, of course -- 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And let me see if I can help you out a little bit. Was this before or after -- it would have been after Dayton -- I mean, after Washington; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I went to Sarajevo after the Dayton Agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: After the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: After the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you moved to Sarajevo, what position did you hold then and at what level?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I was the assistant minister for foreign trade and communications in charge of communications, which is basically the same thing that I did in the Herceg-Bosna government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was this at the state level or was this at the entity level?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: That was at the state level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that would have covered both the Federation and the Republika Srpska and --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the Brcko area, which hadn't become a district yet.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first government, the first joint government set up after the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And again -- moving right along, how long were you in that position?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I remained in that position until I moved to the foreign ministry because I was appointed ambassador to Spain, to the Kingdom of Spain, and that was in early, or rather, April or May 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how long were you an ambassador to Spain?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I was three -- I was in Spain for three and a half years or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And upon your return, what did you do? And if you could just tell us all the way up to the present time very quickly, that is.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, well after that I was an advisor to the president of the Mostar canton or county until I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, when did you retire? When did you retire?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I retired in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But as I understand it, you're still active at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm still active. I do have a very important mission. In Bosnia-Herzegovina there are just a few companies that are operating at the state level, and one of those companies is an independent systems operator. It's a power distribution company that runs the high-tension/high-voltage distribution lines within Bosnia-Herzegovina and those that lead to other countries. And for three and a half years I've been the president of the board of directors and I do have some other activities too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Including gardening as I understand it?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we speak about the activities that you were involved in during the special-purpose council, and I think it's no secret that you were involved primarily in telecommunications, that aspect of it, I would like you to describe to the Trial Chamber how telecommunications worked prior to the war. In fact, you know, if you could even -- if it helps, prior to the break-up of the former Yugoslavia so the Trial Chamber can have an understanding of how the system was working within Yugoslavia and later on with the republic becoming independent.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Could you please tell me if you're asking me this in technical terms or in organizational terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's start with organizational. Just be -- just give us sort of the skeleton, and then technical -- when we get to the technical, I'm more interested in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, in organizational terms in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were several companies, one of them was headquartered in Mostar and it covered the broad territory -- let us put it this way, it was Herzegovina all the way down to Trebinje, to Livno, and to Konjic. It was part of a common system of companies in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was some kind of a holding, that's what you would call it in the West, but it was not a holding as such. They had a high degree of independence. But let us now turn to technical terms. Mostar was one of the 17 nodes in Bosnia-Herzegovina that had a transit exchange. Those nodes were all linked with each other. The link between Mostar and other parts of its area went from the centre to each of those places, like Trebinje, Livno, and so on, and they all had their communications through Mostar. Physically speaking, Mostar had in place a system that was linked up with Sarajevo, it was a coaxial cable that went along the railway line. There were also two large-capacity radio relay systems in place, wireless systems, one went from Mostar to Split and the other went from Mostar to Titograd. So these were the three systems that made it possible for Mostar to establish communications with other areas and enabled others to communication with each other. For instance, Belgrade, if Belgrade wanted to communicate with Split, this went through Mostar; and the same went for, let's say, Skopje and Titograd. So I think that this was a succinct enough explanation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It was. Once Sarajevo -- at one point - we've heard testimony that Sarajevo comes under siege - and so I'll ask you: Did there come a time that the link between Sarajevo and Mostar was cut off?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: It was cut once and for all when the telecommunications centre in Mostar was shelled, that was in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we heard some testimony from before from Mr. Zarko Primorac. As I understand it you know him from your days in Sarajevo, and he was here speaking primarily about financial institutions to -- perhaps it's worth recalling, to what extent are telecommunications important, say, for the banking system, particularly the system that was in place at the time, what is known as the payment bureau, SDK?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, the payment orders between companies could be sent by post or via telecommunications system. It would be unimaginable to use post because it's too slow, so for the most part the telecommunications system was used to link up the banking system and the payments bureau, the SDK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when the linkage between Sarajevo and Mostar is cut off, what were the possibilities of communicating then with Sarajevo? What needed to be done or what could have been done and in fact what was done?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, we could do what we actually did. I don't know what Sarajevo or other areas could have done, but we could first of all establish links between the places that were controlled by the HVO. Secondly, in order to establish a link with the rest of the world we had to establish a link with some place, and at that time the only possible place was Split and that's what we did, step by step, but in the end we were quite successful. As far as Sarajevo was concerned -- well, we always did bear in mind that we wanted to set up a link with Sarajevo, that was always our plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what prevented you from setting up a link with Sarajevo? Was it lack of will or were there other circumstances that made it difficult or impossible?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, in order to set up a link -- well, I have to explain this briefly. Telecommunication lines, large-capacity telecommunication lines used for telephone lines and for data transfer, that's not simple at all. You have to have in place cables that have to be laid in a variety of ways; in order to do that, you have to have land, you have to be able to communicate freely. You could also use radio relay wireless equipment, but the larger the capacity, the smaller the distance must be between various relays. Again, you have to have freedom of movement, control over a territory in order to do this job. You also have to have funds, equipment, and people with the requisite expertise to do it, and there also has to be the will of all the participants in this process to establish this link.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you said that at some point you linked up with Split. Why Split? Why not Zagreb? Why not Ljubljana? Why not Budapest or some other place? Why Split?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I think I've already given you an answer in my previous answer. You have to control the land in order to establish those links. The only area that we controlled where we could move freely was the territory towards Dalmatia. There was no other option except using satellite communication, satellite links, to cover a large distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, would that answer still go for -- for instance, why not link up with Tuzla? Would that be your same answer?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just -- if you could just give us a concrete example. Let's just say that one wanted to make a telephone call to, say, Germany from Mostar, you know, how would the telephone call be placed?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the time-period that you're referring to. At the time when Mostar was destroyed there were no communications in Mostar, but of course as soon as we started with our attempts to set up the communications you did the same thing that you do now, you simply dial a phone number. You could do that in the local area with Croatia, which was a neighbouring country, or everywhere in the world. Any number that was part of this world network could be reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And would that have to go through Split?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness, a small technical question. Did you have connections, telephone links, with Sarajevo using the fax system? Throughout that period were there links or was Mostar totally cut off from the rest of the world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at that time, if you're asking me about Sarajevo, we did not have any communications with them. The telephone lines were down, fax communication was out. At that time we did not have mobile phones, we did not have satellite phones. So to put it quite simply, we had to rely on what we had, cables and radio relay systems that could be used as I explained earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to expand a little bit in that direction. Witness, could you, with a little or as much precision as possible, indicate from which date until which date there was no communication with Sarajevo in the way you have explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Communications with Sarajevo were down at the moment when the communications centre in Mostar was shelled, the communications centre in Mostar, and we simply did not have the capability of establishing communications with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you say at which date that shelling occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know the exact date but I think it was shelled in early -- well, in May 1992. I don't know if I gave the right date. I don't know the exact date, maybe the 15th. It was in May at any rate, the first half of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, and then when did this state of non-communication end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From that time on we put in intensive efforts to set up various communications systems in the areas that we had access to, and in this manner we were able to set up communications not only within Herzegovina itself but using those points that we had access to we were able to establish links between Central Bosnia and Mostar. And likewise, at a point from which you could see Sarajevo, we made it possible for Sarajevo to link up with this network; in other words, for Sarajevo to be linked up with Mostar. And in the first contacts that I myself had with the people in charge in Sarajevo who were dealing with this aspect, we made this offer to them, to establish this communication line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And at what time was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was I think in April 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And did you do that via directional beam aerials? Did the dish antennas went point to point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's how we did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And would broadcast have been a possibility, short-wave, long-wave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let us make some distinctions here. Short-wave and long-wave and ultra-short waves, these are radio channels -- if you want me to, I can explain, these are radio channels used for radio stations that do not need repeaters. Short and medium-wave, you can sometimes do that for the medium-wave --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Long-wave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but for voice transmission you need some capacity. It is not the same if we're talking about 30 lines that can be used at the same time or 100.000 lines that can be open at the same time. The higher the number, the more complexity. For TV signal, you don't need that kind of capacity and you don't need the same kind of equipment for telephone signal transmission and for image transmission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But wouldn't it have been possible to establish some limited radio connection between Sarajevo and Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radio Sarajevo broadcasts at 612 kilohertz and radio Sarajevo broadcasts could be heard in Mostar at all times, but it wasn't always broadcasting or wasn't always operational.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Another question. You have mentioned the possibility of the use of satellites. Now, I understand that was quite some time ago and nothing like today. Could you tell the Chamber to what degree satellite connection was a realistic option at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, satellite communications were used very seldom for telephone transmission -- well, they were probably used for military or some other purposes, but for private users to use this kind of communications -- well, it was just very limited. Today, of course, it's quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can absolutely see that. You make a distinction or one can then make a distinction between, let us say, privileged communications for the government and general possibilities of communications. Were there any special, restricted possibilities of communication between Sarajevo and Mostar that were only accessible to a limited amount of users? You have mentioned the military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that I personally don't know that any of my colleagues had a satellite phone at that time because, as I've already explained, they were hard to come by and the -- and they're very costly to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope I have not anticipated too much, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's okay. That's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I save your time. You must be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's actually -- it throws us off and it causes us more complications, but if we could have the binder because I want to get that last question of yours, Judge Trechsel, because I do think that it might be of some assistance. And I'm going to move in the middle of my presentation to the chapter dealing with telecommunications, PTT.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could go, sir, towards that -- to that section -- if we could -- we'll find it for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for everyone else I'm going to be referring to 1D 00433, and it might be good also to have handy 1D 0432, 1D 0434.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, sir, if we could look at 1D 00433, do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at the top it talks about satellite telephones, as an item we have telephone and fax numbers; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll be seeing another document which makes reference to a contract dated back to 1992. Look at the very first number, we see Alija Izetbegovic. Did you know who Alija Izetbegovic was at the time, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I knew, of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to number 4 because you were asked about special communications, look at number 4, SDA Mostar. What does SDA Mostar mean?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: SDA is the Democratic Action Party. Its president was Alija Izetbegovic. It was one of the parties that won at the democratic election, and the Mostar SDA -- well, that would be the regional centre of that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So here we have the president of the Presidency having a direct link with his Muslim party headquarters in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, if this document is accurate, then yes that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. And we see some other documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, I have a question of curiosity. This document, strange enough, is here in a translation into German --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- can that be explained, please? Also, also, there is something handwritten on the original which has not even a mention in the translation. Was it added later?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: These are the original documents that we got from the Prosecutor, Your Honour. You will then later on see that there is a contract from -- there is some documents from a federal court which I got out of Boston, Massachusetts, because Izetbegovic failed to pay the bill and then claimed that he had no knowledge of it. And what I'm trying to show is that there are some missing links, as it were, but I'm trying to help you out with your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, number 17 we see Zenica. I don't know what the IKB stands for. And of course --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I think it means the Islamic -- it's something to do with Islamic community but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I really can't tell you what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. Now -- and then if we go to the next document, 1D 00432, you know, this is some communications along with a -- with some official documents from the United States District Court, district of Massachusetts, we don't need to go into that, but if you could go to the following document, 1D 00434, we see this is a summons from a civil case. It's addressed to Alija Izetbegovic. We see the address. And we don't have time to go through all of the documents, although I will spell it out at some point, but if everyone can direct their attention to a document which is a letter signed by Alija Izetbegovic. I'm going to read the bottom numbers. In English, it's 1D 24- --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Ibrisimovic wanted to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just being warned that Mr. Puljic [as interpreted] would need to leave for a minute and I would just need to get your permission to allow him to do that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. No problem. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the document -- and I'm going to read a number, Your Honours. It's 1D 24-0512 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Regarding the previous document after all. Witness, Mr. Kozulj, have you ever seen this document before or have you heard about it or can you say anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour -- with all due respect, before you answer the question, if I may be allowed to conduct my direct examination all those questions will be answered. And I don't mean to interrupt. But you've taken me to this direction, now I'm trying to answer your questions, and of course the answer to that question is no. But then if you allow me to continue with my questioning I will be able to answer. I would respectfully request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have limited amount of time, Your Honours, and these interruptions do cause us to spend more time on documents than we wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at this particular document, okay, and I point to point number 3, it says: "I have never signed any kind of purchase agreement or utilisation of satellite telephones in my name. If such agreement exists, it could have been signed only on behalf of PTT Bosnia and Herzegovina or state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whose president and member of the Presidency I was from 1992 to 2000." Now, let's do some foundational questions. First, were you aware that Alija Izetbegovic had this satellite contract and was connected to Mostar SDA, Zenica, and all the other places that are noted on those numbers and faxes? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, but at that time I did hear from some people that there are such satellite telephones that were being used in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, it says here that he would not have -- he did not sign it and wasn't aware of anything. PTT, you indicated you worked there for 13 years. Could you please tell us, based on your background and experience with PTT, would they have been able to sign such a contract in the name of, in the name of, Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: They were not able to do that, no, absolutely no. The PTT would be able to sign or the director of the PTT or some authorised person could have signed a contract on behalf of the PTT organization. Who the funds would be given to for their use, well that's another story altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that this sort of contract would involve a large amount of money, and indeed we do see that at least the services that were unpaid for run close to a million dollars, which at one point meant something. Now -- and of course this is over a period of time. But again, based on your knowledge and experience, would PTT be able to enter into such an agreement with a foreign company without the knowledge of the government, the Presidency, the ministry of -- which oversees PTT? Could PTT have done this all on its own without anyone having any knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: The PTT is a public company under the administration of the government, and I think for something like this, this is quite a major investment and it's an innovation and I think that they would have needed somebody's oral agreement at least to be able to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- and one final question. You did tell us that at some point you were working at the state level, you were working at the state level, after the Dayton Accords. While you were working in that capacity, as I believe you said it was an assistant minister level, dealing specifically with this particular area, that is, telecommunications, were you ever informed that Izetbegovic or PTT, for instance, had engaged in this contract and of course had refused to pay for the services? But I'm primarily interested in whether you had learned that they had actually engaged in this contract.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I never found out about it and I was never informed about it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I have no further questions on this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If, Judge Trechsel, you wish to supplement concerning the satellite phones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No I think that's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we wish to get certified copies from the US courthouse, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we were talking about telecommunications. You went into more detail than we wanted at this point, but I think it's useful. Now I want to switch your attention a little bit again for general purposes to the issue of electricity. You told us the current position you hold. You've told us that you were an electrical engineer. I assume that you studied electricity, you know, when you got your degree. If you could please tell us in general how the electrical system worked in Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to the war. Just give us the same thing that you did with telecommunications, do that with electricity now.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, in the organizational aspect first. The electrical system has three main activities: The manufacture of electricity, this could be hydro-electric power-plants, thermal power-plants, nuclear power-plants, at the time we only had the hydro-electric power-plants and the thermal power-plants; then you would have the power distribution to households and to companies; the third area would be the transmission of electricity from the place it was being manufactured to the distribution centres. The electrical utilities in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were organized at the time in a way that you had distribution companies, there were some production companies, and also there was a separate company for the transmission of electrical -- of electricity whose headquarters were in Sarajevo. When you look at Mostar, its electrical distribution company was headquartered there and then you had one power-plant as part of it, then you had the transmission from the place of production to the distribution points, and there was also a part of the company on the Neretva River that had a number of hydro-electric power-plants along the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: At the same time, this is also a technical aspect, energy is being produced at the hydro-electric or thermal-electric power-plants and then through the transmission systems and transmission stations, it would be transmitted throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina and then was being distributed through the transformer stations to their end users. So this organization or this structure had multiple links, it has alternate routes, and also is linked to neighbouring republics as well as neighbouring states.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: It is a unified European system, it's part of the European grid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, first things first. You said that it would be linked to its neighbouring countries or republics. To what extent it was linked to Croatia? And could you please explain that to us, especially from the -- in and around the Mostar area, Herzegovina, that part.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, it was linked in several ways. The actual structure was technically connected with the transmission -- power transmission lines at different levels. Mostar had a transmission -- a transformer station which was a very important one and a very rare one which can take the power of 400 kilovolts. It was very important because it had links to Bosnia via Sarajevo and then also through Bosnia with other eastern republics, and then with Croatia there was a -- also a number of transmission, power transmission lines. There were also -- there were also lower-voltage transmission lines and both of them were being used. There is also a joint interest of the power manufacturing industry between, let's say, Croatia, Bosnia, and Serbia. For example, if there is a power-plant on the river Drina, it would deliver power to Bosnia and Serbia, so that would be their mutual interest. For example, if there was a power-plant on the river Cetina near Omis, it would be using the reservoir from the area of Bosnia in the Tomislavgrad and Livno municipalities. Also the power-plant Plat near Dubrovnik would use water from the Trebinje and Bileca areas which were in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As far as I know, Croatian power -- the Croatian power industry invested in thermo-electricity plants in Tuzla and some other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So there were multiple interests in this sense, but in any case the systems were technically connected in order to be able to use the energy available in a synergistic manner in order that we could help each other if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, was the system in any way damaged during the war in 1992 in Mostar; and if so, to what extent?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: The system was vulnerable in two ways. For example, the transmission stations, not only the actual stations but the component parts that make it run were -- also sub-stations, et cetera, were attacked and destroyed, several transformer stations around Mostar were destroyed. The other element are power transmission lines which cover large territories, they're usually in inaccessible areas, they go over hills where there are no paths. And because of some malfunction or because they were destroyed, they were put out of operation and it was difficult to get to them to be able to repair them. So at one point in time Mostar had a shortage of electricity, they had less available than the city needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the linkage between Mostar and Sarajevo, was there -- did there ever come a time when there was a break in that linkage?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: It was cut. I cannot say whether it was -- the connection was broken because it was due to a malfunction or because it was cut off. We had a shortage of electricity because the area of Herzegovina only had one power-plant that was operating and that could have been used to provide electricity, that is the Capljina plant which -- it's a hydro-electric power-plant which depended on water and it depended on the weather conditions. So this water was under the control of the Serb forces at that time, and that whole region was not properly supplied with electricity. The output was very low, and if there were moments when there was an abundance of water then the electricity supply would be much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That will do for now as far as the general questions on electricity, and unless there are any questions I'm going to go right into the documents. Okay. If we could -- we'll start at the beginning of your binder and I'm going to be going through the first batch, the first chapter deals primarily with events that occurred when you were with the special-purpose council. And we'll move through the first few documents rather quickly. The first document is P 00190, we see it's dated 7 May 1992, and we see at the very -- under number 1: "I hereby appoint the special-purpose council of the Mostar municipal staff ..." And we see your name, number 4, Ilija Kozulj, that's you?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And of course if we go under number 2, 2(a), we see the list of activities, but you did discuss to us what the activities that you were involved in. Before leaving this document if you could please tell us to your understanding the Mostar municipal staff at that point in time, what is it being referred to, a civil organ or a military organ?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I think that it was a military organ at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 02716, and this is dated 9 May 1992, we see that this is a certificate. You do see your name, do you not, sir, on the very first line?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it says that you are there to assist, you can move around for the purposes of establishing and maintaining the communication system. If we look at who signed this document, it says: "Head of communications, captain first class," and I believe it says Jure Zadro; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Jure Zadro, yes, the late Jure Zadro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And with this certificate I take it you were able to go about your business to some extent for the special-purpose council, that is?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I was in a way invited to a meeting there and I was asked to help to resolve these matters and I accepted that, and then he gave me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. P 00209, this is six days later, this is dated 15 May 1992. We see at the very top of the page there is a reference to PTT in regards to everything else that's either malfunctioning or has been damaged. But most importantly for us is if we look at the section where it says: "Order," and the order -- we've seen this document before. 1 disbands the Crisis Staff, and it then says that the municipal -- the Mostar municipal staff will form a civilian wartime government. And then number 3, which is what we're mostly interested in, it says: "Until the government referred to in paragraph 2 of this order is formed, The Special-purpose Council of the Mostar municipality staff of the Croatian Defence Council shall administer the entire functioning of the city and care for its citizens." Now -- and it's signed by president of the Mostar municipal staff, Jadran Topic. My first question is: Were you aware of this particular order at the time?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I was aware of it. We didn't read it, but I was familiar with it. I knew that there was such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how did you understand this order when it says that the special-purpose council, of which you were one of I believe 12 or 13 members, were to administer the entire functioning of the city and care for its citizens? How did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I understood that to mean -- well, first of all I think that it wasn't realistic for us to take care of all the civilian matters of the town. I think that we didn't have the means or the staff at our disposal for that, but I do think that we could have - and that is what we did, and that was to discuss how the civilian affairs in town should be organized and we proposed how this should be done. So from that aspect, that is how I understood this assignment. I am conveying this to you and then it's up to you to suggest or to propose how this should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go now to 1D 02743, and -- okay. Have you seen this document before, sir?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I think they didn't discuss this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I cannot be sure that I did see it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One step at a time. If we can go step by step.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Very well, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing this document before?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I cannot remember clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the very top it says: "Special Purpose Council of the Municipal Staff of HVO Mostar at the sessions held on 15th and 19th May, 1992 ..." and then it goes on. And then on the third paragraph it talks about: "Apart from this task, it is necessary to redefine the structure and competencies of the Crisis Staff (former name), which would consolidate and manage the town in all aspects, and substitute in war conditions, the democratically elected civilian governing bodies." All right. Now, in coming here today have you had a chance to look at this document; and if so, would you please explain to us what you understand this document purports to be?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I said that I'm not sure if I've seen this document or not, but I am sure that I participated in meetings and in conversations about how to organize this. I don't know who drafted the document. I didn't. Second, according to my understanding, this decision constitutes a proposal how to organize the civilian authority in the town of Mostar in the then-prevailing conditions so that most of these sectors are a part of the town of business and the matters that the town authorities deal with. Some of these sections perhaps exceed that level, but -- in my view, but there was no other option, I'm thinking of item 3. I think this is a matter for the prosecutor's office or courts. This is something that was usually dealt with at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said decision -- this is not a decision, this is actually --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: This is just a draft. I made a mistake. It's just a plain draft. It's not signed. It's just thoughts on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go on to the next document, 1D 02743 -- I'm sorry, to the next document which is P 00219, my apologies, we see now this is 21 May 1992, this would have been a couple of days at least from the last meeting which was on the 19th of May, as reflected in the earlier document. Here now we see a decision by Jadran Topic, and of course here it appears that he's establishing the Croatian Defence Council of Mostar municipality and he lists the various positions. Having looked at this decision and having looked at the previous document, do you see any similarities?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Jadran Topic used the proposal by -- that was drafted by the special-purpose council in drafting this particular decision?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I believe so, yes. I'm convinced that this was used or at least was used or at least was something that was consulted on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when we look at this particular decision, assuming that you are competent based on having grown up in the system and having worked in the system, can you please tell us whether the formation of the government, as is reflected in this decision, P 00219, were there any similarities with the previous system that had existed, that is, prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: It does, almost entirely. It does reflect that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document P 002 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. The next document will be after the break. It's time for a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing's resumed. My fellow Judge is going to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm truly sorry that I have interfered with your course because I understand your concern. I was not aware of it. I invite you, if you have the feeling that I'm going in that direction again to interrupt me and say, Just hold it, I'm going into all that, and I will accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is I who should be apologising, Judge Trechsel. I think I was a little exuberant in my response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have been worse at other times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm still working on that, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: P 00221, P 00221, here we see -- this was a decision based on the earlier decision that we saw, and these were the actual individuals that were appointed, and as I understand it from your previous answers that you were not participating in a formal capacity with this civilian government; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. Now we go to the next document, 1D 02390, and this is a report that was authored by Dr. Jadranko Prlic. It is dated 4 June 1992. It's -- and you see that he signed it as general manager of Apro Corporation Mostar. First of all, did you know at the time Dr. Jadranko Prlic, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Second, did you know this Apro Corporation Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please very briefly tell us about this corporation.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: It was a large corporation that mostly was involved in agri business. It had vineyards and orchards, it had several wine production plants, and it also manufactured various components for food industry, for juices and so on. And it was a large enterprise headquartered in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many people were employed in this corporation and its various holdings?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I can't be sure but a couple of thousand people, but the number of employees would go up with seasonal workers when there was farm work to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, this is a report, and it's directed to the department for the economy, again dated 4 June 1992. Do you know whether at that time other such corporations had to make similar reports to the department of economy, keeping in mind the events that were unfolding at the time?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, usually such reports were sent. I don't know whether they were under an obligation to do so, but that's what they did because the head of the department wanted to be made -- informed about the situation in the economy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: We did not catch the name of the head of the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, who was the head of the department at the time, did you know, the department of economy?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Mr. Senad Kazalic was the head of the department for economy, he was also the chairman of the special-purpose council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were -- at that period of time, in light of the circumstances, given that you had a Crisis Staff before and now you have the new situation involving -- were local corporations, companies, obligated to assist in providing various resources, human or otherwise, towards the war effort?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, because first of all, all the companies got the directors appointed. If the previous directors were now absent, new directors had to be appointed. They usually wanted to get a certain number of employees in order to be able to perform their tasks with the minimum number of staff, and that is why they wanted to get the lists of people under the work obligation. And of course they had to place themselves at the disposal for defence preparations. This is how things were in our country before this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document, 1D 02715, this is dated 10 June 1992 and we see that it's by Commander Major Jasmin Jaganjac, and it's the Croatian Defence Council, municipal staff Mostar. And it says here that you as a member of the special-purpose council are empowered to carry out necessary activities on behalf of this staff. Can you explain this a little bit? Obviously you must have known who Mr. Jaganjac was?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Jaganjac was the military commander in Mostar, and he was also a member of the Mostar government, if I can call it that, the administration in Mostar. This order merely served to reinforce the previous one and it brought all these things closer to the obligations towards the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 02714, this document is dated 20 June 1992, 1D 02714. This is an order and this is signed by the head of the council, Dinko Slezak, and here we see your name and you are being tasked, as it were, to draft a programme for the work, planning, recovery, and development of telecommunication systems and radio and TV network for Mostar and surrounding area. Do you know Mr. Slezak?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I do know Mr. Slezak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And based on this particular order, did you engage in any activities that were being suggested, that is, in drafting a programme for the work and planning, recovery, and development of telecommunication systems in and around the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, together with the gentlemen who are mentioned here, Enes Santic worked in the Mostar post and telecommunications, and Mr. Zvonimir Trlen [phoen], it says Enes here but his name is actually Zvonimir, he was the director of UNIS telecom which manufactured telecommunications equipment, and Mr. Jasenko Lasta, he was an engineer, he worked in radio and television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I coordinated the work on this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say that you were probably the most experienced of -- among the group?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, given my age.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. You're being very modest. And Mr. Enes himself, what nationality is this gentleman, Enes Santic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, it's Bosniak in the current parlance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And we mean no disrespect by that. 1D 02669, 1D 02669, this is dated 26 August 1992. We see this is a list of HVO municipal staff Mostar wounded, and if we go to the bottom of the page we see your name, it says: "The representatives of HVO Municipal Staff Mostar who visited the above listed wounded soldiers ..." And we see your name, Ilija Kozulj, Slavko Puljic, Jure Maric, Mr. Ivan Udovicic, Drazen, Vucina, and Franjo Petric. And then if we go to the second page in English or if we continue on it says: "On that occasion the wounded soldiers were given radio sets ..." and so on and so forth. Do you recall this particular visit? Could you please tell us a little bit about it, especially with respect to the radio sets?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this visit. In cooperation with the UNIS companies, I obtained a certain number of small transistor radios and we decided that the best thing to do would be to give them to the soldiers hospitalised in Split because that would make it possible for them to keep in touch with the current events, and that's what we did. We distributed those transistor radios to the soldiers who were there -- at least that's what we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we've gone over this list together and I'm going to read out some names and I'm going to ask you to confirm this. Of the list of 33 do we see names that are -- of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Quite a few of them in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I were to go down the list, number 2, number 4, number 5, number 9, number 10, number 11, number 22, 23, 25, 27, 28, 29, to your knowledge, knowing the names in that region, do these appear to be Muslim members of the HVO municipal staff Mostar, at least as of 26th August 1992?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, those are Muslim members of the Mostar HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 02666 dated 27 August 1992, we see there is an order, we see it's to you, and you're being asked to organize parts of UNIS and it's head -- it's signed by the head of department of economy Vlado Soljic. I'm doing the best I can with these names. Now, you obviously know Mr. Soljic, right?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Mr. Soljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And of course -- before we go through the various parts of UNIS, if we look at the very first part, very first paragraph, it says here: "On the basis of the decision of Herceg-Bosna HVO to form entities - out of all segments of business systems, whose headquarters were in Sarajevo and other parts of the Republic of BiH, as well as in other republics - which will function independently, until the end of the war and the establishment of the democratic government, in the entire territory of the Republic of BiH ..." And then we see this. Based on just this first paragraph that I read, what was your understanding of what you were being asked to do?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: As a member of the UNIS board of directors, I was in charge of some of the companies that are mentioned here, not all of them, but here I was asked to make sure that these companies could be reorganized temporarily until it was possible for them to link up with their head office in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And more or less these companies, what are they involved in? We can see the first one, it's electronics. One is a joint investment, a telecommunications joint investment, what does UNIS TBM, what is that about, the joint-stock company?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: It manufactured office equipment, mostly typewriters and cash registers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about UNIS Unidata?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: UNIS Unidata was a company that did information technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, keeping this order in mind let's look at the next document, 1D 02664 -- I'm sorry, 2665, I apologise, because at the bottom we see your name and it is addressed to a Mr. Faruk Smailbegovic - I think I got that right - do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you know the gentleman?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do. While I was a member of the board of directors in UNIS in charge of electronics, office equipment, and telecommunications, he was in charge of the companies that manufactured cars and car parts within the UNIS group. At this time I think he was the president of UNIS, and he was also a minister in the BH government and his portfolio was economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we do not see a date on this document, but if we look at -- the previous document was dated 27 August 1992. You were told to organize certain -- to reorganize certain parts of UNIS, and if we look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, in the B/C/S document there is a date, 27th of August, so it seems -- no, you're right, that's the next document. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the one that's undated, that is, 1D 02665, and we look at the letter, at the risk of asking a leading question, would it appear that this letter is in connection with the previous document, 1D 02666?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, it is connected with it because it deals with the same issue, and I think that this letter was sent in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And in this you do point out that HVO Mostar has confirmed certain appointments, a Mr. Emir Peco, a Veid Hakalo. These two individuals, are they Muslim or are they Croat?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: They are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And before we leave this document, did Mr. Faruk Smailbegovic ever get back to you on this particular correspondence?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Unfortunately, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. When was the next time -- before I -- before the next question let me ask this: How would this letter have gone to the gentleman? We know that telecommunications were out. Was the postal service working? In other words, could you put a stamp and go to the mailbox and mail it off?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: No, no. It was not possible to do so. I made use of some kind of humanitarian relief. A truck was heading to Sarajevo carrying humanitarian aid, and I asked them to take some gifts to some people in Sarajevo and also this letter to Mr. Smailbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. When was the next time that you met this gentleman?
