utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: At one point the delegation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina government visited Mostar and we held talks with them, and Mr. Smailbegovic was in that delegation. I think it was in 1994 if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Early 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I think we're going to get to that topic later on. If we go to the next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A short question regarding the dates, Witness. You on 27th of August are ordered to file a report within 30 days; is that correct? That's the document 2666.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Now you sent an analogous, or next step as it were, order to Sarajevo and you set also a time-limit of 30 days; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In the letter we are dealing with now, 2665, addressed to Mr. Faruk Smailbegovic, you also tell him he was to report -- or I thought I had seen that he was to report within 30 days but maybe that's an error of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It is an error. I deeply apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see that. At any rate, I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It would have been rather presumptuous to order the president, your supervisor. But this letter, 1D 02665, if we look at the second-to-last paragraph where you say: "You are kindly requested to take note of the above stated and make sure that it is accepted from the UNIS level and that no actions are taken which may adversely influence the functioning of the companies and my work ..." And then you say rather directly: "Quite contrary, I expect that your work and influence will be positive and useful. I especially hope that there will be soon a possibility to communicate in an appropriate way." Perhaps in light of the question from Judge Trechsel you can explain to us what exactly you were asking Mr. Smailbegovic to do.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: First of all, I wanted to inform him about the situation. Secondly, in light of the situation that we faced, we wanted him to accept it and not to cause any problems because I thought it was the decent thing to do. Third, I asked him to assist, to facilitate the work of those companies if possible. And finally, I expressed my wish that our communication would proceed along better lines in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I think that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we go to the next document, 1D 02667, here we have a document from the director Nenad Dasovic. This is for permission to enter a UNIS location for employees of TAMP company. And we see the list of names. It's dated 15 October 1992. Are you familiar with TAMP company?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the names now, again this is 15 October 1992, and I'm going to ask you whether you would agree with me numbers 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, and 12 are Muslim names.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Those are indeed Muslim names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And this particular company, what did it do, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: This company manufactured various metal and plastic parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Next document, just so we -- moving right along time-wise on this, 1D 02396, dated 22 October 1992, this is a special permit and we see that it's for Mr. Camil Salahovic, and he's being granted freedom of movement in Mostar municipality during the curfew. Now, did you know Mr. Salahovic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I knew him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, right. And he is a lawyer, right?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he's also Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, he's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at that time as I understand it he was also involved in SDA politics, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was involved in SDA politics, but he was also a member of the special-purpose council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it in order -- could you move about Mostar after curfew -- during the -- after curfew?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I couldn't move about --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Without a special permit?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I couldn't move about without a special permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Why was it necessary to have a special permit at the time to move about during the curfew, do you know? What were the conditions in Mostar, in other words?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, the conditions were -- well, there was shelling, so there was no pressing need for anyone to move about the town apart from military personnel who were going about their business. So there was no need for people to walk about and to cause all kinds of problems. If there were people moving about without any obvious need, then it might be that they had some nefarious purpose. So movement was restricted during the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Next document -- next three documents go to appointments, 1D 00665, this is a decision to appoint the temporary director of UNIS UTP, and it's Emir Peco who is a mechanical engineer. You know this gentleman, do you not?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we can see this is dated 23 November 1992, and this gentleman was a Muslim, was he not or is?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 00690, this is dated 6 January 1993. This is to appoint an interim director for UNIS Racunari company and this is for Ibrahim Mutisevic. First of all, do you know this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Mutisevic. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he's a Muslim, is he not?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can you please tell us, what does this particular company do?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: This company manufactured computer equipment, computers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: And also provided computer-related services.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the last document in this area is 1D 00692. This is a decision to appoint an acting director UNIS UTT, and I believe it should be UTP. This is Mirsad Derviskadic.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Derviskadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that should be UNIS UTP, correct, not UTT?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What does this company do?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: This company manufactured special electrodes in cooperation with the German company UTP. That is why it was called UTP because it was a joint venture. Germans invested some money into this company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on now to the next chapter and this deals with public enterprises and I'm not going to ask you to describe the difference between a public enterprise and a socially owned enterprise, although if the Bench has any questions on that I'm sure they'll ask you. If we look at the first document, 1D 02754, 1D 02754, this is a Law on Financing the Public Services. This is dated 1990. Were you aware of this particular law and how it functioned?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I do know the basic things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at Article 3, for instance, it talks about: "The offices responsible for funding public services pursuant to this law are: The Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." it then goes on, "assemblies of socio-political communities ..." And so and so forth. Briefly, what is a socio-political community?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Socio-political communities are actually a unit of government in a certain area, local communes, or the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at Article 4 it says municipal public services -- I'm going to have to ask you to repeat your answer. I don't know whether this was translated or not, I wasn't paying attention to be honest, to the question about what is a socio-political community. So could you please tell us -- give us that definition again so we can get it clearly on the record. And I'm going to ask you to speak a little slower, and my apologies for speaking so fast and rushing you.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Socio-political communities cover a certain territory. A local commune is a basic socio-political community. It does not have any power or attributes of power, but it is there to communicate with the people. And then the next level up is the municipality. It cannot exercise -- it does exercise power --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and then the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time was the highest level in accordance with this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I could focus your attention on Article 4, just very briefly, it says: "Municipal public services funded pursuant to this law include," and then we see a list of services, and I just want to focus everyone's attention, and especially yours where it says: "Municipal obligations created by the establishment of public enterprises." What does that mean for those of us who are not familiar with the system there?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: The municipality is duty-bound to found public companies for the needs of its citizens. It owns those enterprises, manages them, and determines how they will do their business and it establishes the prices at which they will work if they provide services that they charge for, and then they -- it also helps them in case they need investment assistance or if they sustain losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll go on to the next document 1D 00568, this is dated 19 June 1992. This is a decision governing the functioning of the town utility services in conditions of war, and I want to focus your attention to Article 2 because we see -- and it lists three particular services: Electrical power-supply; water-supply, and waste water disposal; and collection and disposal of garbage, undertaker services, town dog pound, and other utility services. Are you familiar with this particular decision, sir?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to Article 4, maybe you could help us out a little bit. Article 4 says that: "Elektrohercegovina and the Elektroprijenos plant in Mostar shall operate as regional enterprises, I underscore regional enterprises. Could you help us how the, what is meant by regional enterprises?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Elektrohercegovina with headquarters in Mostar is a company that manufactured and distributed electricity in the entire territory from Livno to Trebinje and Konjic, so it was like the PTT company. The Elektroprijenos company was a separate company with headquarters in Sarajevo which distributed -- or actually brought the electricity from the manufacturer via the transformer stations to the end users using transformer stations and high-voltage and low-voltage transmission power lines for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One last point, on Article 14, help us out here a little bit, if we look at the third paragraph under Article 14, and of course you have to look at the previous two paragraphs but I'm focusing on the last part, which says: "The employees on stand-by shall enjoy the same rights as all other workers on stand-by in the municipality of Mostar." What are they talking about, stand-by, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Sometimes because of the lower volume or reduced volume of work, not all personnel is required to be at work the whole time. So a number is at work and do have work duty in these conditions, while others are at home and are waiting to be summoned in case there is a need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When it says that they have the same rights as all other workers on stand-by in the municipality of Mostar, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: In peacetime when a company sends its workers home on stand-by, then the question of compensation has to be resolved during that period. During wartime there was solidarity and the attempt was made to give equal rights for compensation to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: All those on stand-by of course, all those on stand-by have equal rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00569, this is a decision on transport, telecommunication, and information. And it's dated 19 June 1992. It says under Article 1: "In order to ensure the maintenance and functioning of the transport, telecommunication, and information system under wartime conditions ..." And it goes on. And Article 2: "Under this decision, transport, telecommunications, and information system shall encompass the following ..." And we see a list including mail services, telecommunications services, transport on rivers, and so on. Were you familiar with this particular decision; and if so, why was it necessary to pass this decision? One would expect that life could go on without such decisions being passed.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: At the time it was essential to organize life in some fashion. In Mostar there were parts of different companies or entire companies covering these particular sectors. There had to be some decision to place all those people in organizations under supervision and to issue assignments to them so that they could work towards the defence of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to Article 13 particularly, it talks about telecommunications. And I want to focus your attention, I'll read this as best I can. "The Postanski Promet Herceg-Bosna enterprise of Mostar shall organize telecommunications in," this is the part that we're interested in, "Jablanica, Konjic, Prozor, Posusje, Siroki Brijeg, Citluk, Ljubuski, Grude, Neum, Capljina, Stolac, Ljubinje, Nevesinje, and Ravno ..." Could you please explain to us why these particular areas -- can you interpret this for us and why not say other areas as well, Tuzla -- I don't even see Mostar here.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Mostar is implied most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: This decision in my view is not the best drafted decision, but it was necessary to say that the company with headquarters in Mostar, and before the war it was the PTT enterprise, would be obliged to provide these services in the areas. It couldn't provide services in its earlier area before but only in the free area, free territory. So the municipalities or parts of municipalities that were free at that time are referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 00872, 1D 00872, this is a decision on temporary registration and business activities of the Tuzla public railway transport enterprise. And of course I'm showing you this because we want to make some comparisons, and we see that Article 1, the Tuzla Public Railway Transport Enterprise, with its head office in Tuzla, shall organize, and so on. Article 2 says: "The court of registration in Tuzla is hereby instructed to temporarily register the entity referenced in Article 1 ..." and so on. Have you had a chance to look at this decision and can you please comment on this? And I'm specifically interested to know whether Tuzla prior to the war, Tuzla municipality, could have passed this sort of a decision, was it competent?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Before the war the municipality of Tuzla was not authorised to make such decisions. These are jobs regulated by republican law. However, in war conditions they had to organize railway traffic in some manner, and this was one of the ways to do that, the only way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, having looked at the previous documents on organizing or reorganizing in the Mostar area and we look at this particular decision, is Tuzla doing anything different as reflected in this document than, say, Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: This is the same thing. The text is different but it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: It's formulated differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at 1D 00350, this now is dated 4 May 1993. It's -- we can see that this was passed by the War Presidency of Jablanica. If we look at the very end of the document we see the name of Safet Cibo, I believe he's a doctor -- I believe he's a medical doctor in fact, we see this decision. Have you had a chance to look at this particular decision?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I looked at it when I received it. Now I can look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, perhaps, Witness, you could tell us when you received it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lawyer showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me -- this document was shown to you for the purposes of comparing this document with what's happening in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You had no contact with Mr. Cibo at the time?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: No, no, no. I have no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Based on your background and experience -- based on your background and experience, because it does talk about energy system, it talks about Elketrojablanica, do you think you're competent to discuss the contents in this document in relation to the previous document shown to you say in regards to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I don't know what the question would be but, yes, I can talk about things like this. If -- if ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Here I can see that this is the same decision as the one in Tuzla and the one in Mostar. It's phrased differently, the text is different, but it boils down to the president of the War Presidency of Jablanica decides that parts of former companies from the electrical utility company and the hydro-electrical plant on the Neretva and the Elektroprijenos company headquartered in Sarajevo should unite or merge into one company because there was no other way to organize the electricity power-supply unless all the elements were brought together under one umbrella.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at this a little closer. Now, we know that Cibo -- we can see that he's the president of both Jablanica and Konjic, and if we look at Article 7, for instance, it says: "As a result of this decision, the authorities of the current electric power-plants and of their managers over the electric power-plant buildings in the area of Jablanica and Konjic municipalities shall cease to exist, with the exception of Elektroprivreda BiH, Sarajevo enterprise, which is assumed to retain responsibility for the exploitation and the coordination of the work of the facilities." My question is: You having worked in this area and knowing how things have worked in BiH, prior to the war or should I say if there were no warlike conditions and there was no War Presidency, assuming Dr. Cibo was a duly elected president of Jablanica or Konjic municipality - and I say that for a purpose because he was appointed by Izetbegovic - but assuming that this was a knock-on situation would the president of the municipality have the capacity, the ability, the right to issue such a decision, keeping in mind Article 7?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: No, no way. The president of the municipality could not do that because this would have been regulated by a law of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but in wartime conditions one does what one has to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at another chapter. Now I'm going to deal a little bit with electrical power, and we're going to go to 1D 00566. This is dated 19 June 1992. This is a decision to establish a provisional list of priorities for electric power-supply, and we see the various places starting off with the hospital, moving down we see the post office, and so on. And could you please tell us why was it necessary at that time to your understanding to have such a priority list?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Because of the destruction caused by war and the inaccessibility of some facilities, Mostar suffered the shortage of power in some parts of the town, and that is why power cuts were put in place and power was supplied only to those who really needed it at times when there simply was not enough power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at Roman numeral II it says: "The Elektrohercegovina, EP, electric power company, Mostar, shall be responsible for the implementation of this decision." Were you familiar with this particular company, sir?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, it's a company that was in generation -- power generation and power distribution, and it covered the whole of Herzegovina, delineated by Trebinje, Livno, and Konjic, and it was headquartered in Mostar as I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So this would be a regional company then?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, it was a regional company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00589, 3 July 1992, this is a decision on the temporary delivery of electricity to the Republic of Croatia, and we're going to park over here and discuss this a little bit. We see from this document that it says first of all: "Since the Republic of Croatia has repaired the power system of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and because the Neretva River basin has been prepared and we can transfer and distribute electricity ..." then if we go on obviously we see that this is a decision to deliver power to the Republic of Croatia. Could you please explain to us what is happening in this decision, assuming that you're -- you have the necessary background knowledge and information to do so.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I see that the question arises: How is it possible to supply power to other parties if you don't have enough power in the town of Mostar itself, but you have to bear in mind that these are generation capacities, the hydro-electric power-plants, that are dependent on the amount of water in the rivers. At times hydro-electric power-plants are able to work at top capacity. Sometimes they have to because of the influx of water it would be a pity not to use all that water coming in, whereas at times they cannot operate at all because there is simply not enough water. The situation with thermo-electric power-plants is different, they provide a stable supply of electricity. Now, the Mostar region at that time had several hydro-electric power-plants. At times it had a surplus of power, and it is possible that some parts of the town, because the transmission lines were low capacity, could not get enough power despite the fact that there was enough power in the system because the transformers were not -- did not have a high capacity. And there was a -- this need to deliver the surplus power elsewhere because at times when there was not enough power in Herzegovina it had to be imported from somewhere, and the only place where it could be imported from was Dalmatia. So you had two weak partners that had to help each other. When one partner had a surplus of power, it delivered the power to the other partner. That's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And was that the case prior to the conflict, prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, it was always the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Unless there are any questions on this I'll move on to the next document, 1D 01804 [Realtime transcript read in error "01084"]. Now, we saw this document with our previous witness but again I want to show it to you. This is dated 5 August 1992. We've seen the gentleman's name, Vladimir Colic.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course he's talking about -- it's from the very first paragraph. We see: "The decree of the Presidency of the HVO ... determines among other things (the establishment of the Elektroprivreda public enterprise of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna ..." And then there is a list of reasons, justifications, but I'm most interested in you commenting on this letter after looking at the very last paragraph where he says: "Lastly, it should be pointed out that the observations about the real situation in BH, the identified tasks on links power grid segments in the region of HZ BH and the fact that the power grid of HZ will be connected to the entire power grid of RBH do not prejudice any political solutions after the war and that all that is being done is for the benefit of all citizens of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and BH." Now, first, I've shown you this document; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Before it disappears, it's purely technical, in the record it says 1D 01084 but it is 1D 01804.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. 1D 01804.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- familiar with the events that are being described, especially at the very top of the page, by Mr. Soljic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in your estimation the proposal that Mr. Soljic is making through this letter, can you comment on that, keeping in mind the very last paragraph that I read.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Soljic says that because of the situation it is necessary to set up a public company, electric utility of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, to organize life, and to ensure regular supply -- regular power-supply, and he also gives some practical conclusions as to how this should be done, saying that this does not prejudice the final organization of the electric power sector, saying that this would be set up at a later date once there is peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, does that make sense what he's saying?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Of course it makes sense. This means that now we are forced to set up this public company and later on we will see how we will deal with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Was Sarajevo in a position at that point in time, given the conditions in Sarajevo and -- in and around it, that is, and the conditions in Mostar, was it possible for Sarajevo to have provided some alternative proposal, some alternative arrangement that would have benefitted each and all?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't see a possibility for that. Secondly, let us not forget that Elektrohecegovina, even before the war, was highly independent within the electric power system in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It enjoyed a high degree of independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there a question from the Bench? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 00017, this is a decision on the establishment of the public electricity supply enterprise. Okay. This is dated -- as I understand it, it's from the session of the 28th of August, 1992, and it's by Dr. Jadranko Prlic who was serving as the president of the HVO HZ HB. Can you please explain to us why was it necessary for this particular decision to be passed. How do we account for this?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: It was necessary because we had a company, Elektrohecegovina, in Mostar which was quite independent but the other aspect, the transmission of power, the Elektroprijenos company, was headquartered in Sarajevo. And it only had its plant there in that area, it was not independent at all, autonomous at all. It was necessary to merge all those companies together into a single power utility, to merge them in order to be able to control it and manage it and also assist it in meeting its function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: But I have to say here that in a way the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna included some other areas that were not in Herzegovina, some other parts of the company that were not in Herzegovina, such as Central Bosnia and Posavina, and somebody had to take care of them. And this was all done by a single company in order to achieve the best results possible and to have cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. When you said that it was necessary to merge, is that because the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is trying to absorb these competencies, take over, or was it due to the circumstances as a result of the war conditions on the ground? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand. From whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I mean, there may be arguments being made that these were efforts by -- hear me out, these were efforts made by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to take over for the purposes of establishing itself as an independent state, a state within a state. And my question is: Could it be -- could this be interpreted for those reasons or was it necessary to merge because of the conditions that were unfolding on the ground, the war, the siege in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: It was absolutely necessary to do that. I don't know how many times is it necessary to explain this. You have segments of various companies that are located in a certain territory. This territory cannot survive, cannot subsist, without power and you have to link up all those elements. The best way, indeed the only way, is to merge them into a single organization. And finally I have to say that every public company is a territorial organization that meets the needs of the people in a certain area, and in the final analysis it is the -- it is owned by the people in that area. So when you say, Did you take over or did you seize it, you cannot do it because it belongs to the people living in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at Article 2, the name of this is Elektroprivreda of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. What is the name -- first of all, does this company exist today; and if so, under what name?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: This company exists and it is still operating under the same name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Elektroprivreda of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at Article 4 it says: "The public enterprise shall ensure ..." and one, two, three -- the fourth point it says that "The system of electricity supply of Herceg-Bosna is interlinked both within the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and outside the Republic." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What is meant by that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: That means that this company, for reasons that I've already stated, must be linked up within Bosnia and Herzegovina wherever possible and also with areas outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina wherever that is feasible. This is a requirement because of the technology used in power industry, and -- so this was done whenever it was possible, whenever it was feasible. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00097, this is 8 September 1992, this is a decision on the approval of the enactments of HZ BH public electrical utility enterprise. What is this about? Why is this decision necessary in light of the previous decision that we looked at?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: The company has to pass its statute that will form the basis for its operation; statute deals with a number of issues from the organization, the sphere of activity, the management, funding, and so on. This statute has to be submitted by the company to the founder, in this case the company was founded by the Government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This company had to submit its statute for approval. Likewise, the prices, the rates, for the services are also approved by the founder, in this case it was the Government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So this decision indicates that the Government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna indeed adopted those two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 02444, 1D 02444. We saw an earlier document where Mr. Topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Karnavas, before you continue. You said that you needed two hours. You have already used up two hours and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I said -- first I have him down for three hours. I then indicated that I would try to do him in two hours. I don't know how I can be any more efficient. I would have liked to have done him in two hours, to finish this witness in two hours. It looks like I might need an extra 30 minutes or whatever, but I certainly will be within the three-hour period. Secondly, if I may answer the issues that were brought up before the gentleman entered the courtroom, we do intend to provide you with a list, you and the other members of the Bench, as well as the Prosecution -- we did with our entire list of witnesses for the remainder of our defence case with the hours. We will endeavour to stay within that -- those limitations, those hour limitations, and we are very mindful that we need to reserve some time for other witnesses by other Defences. So my apologies if I was misunderstood, but I would have liked to have done him in two hours. Unless we're going to break at this moment I'm going to continue. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 02444, if we look at this document, it's 16 October 1992, and this is a request for payment based on the charge of the use of the Busko Lake dam reservoir. And obviously: "We hereby request the Croatian Electricity Supply Board to settle immediately the claim ..." We see this is from the municipality of Tomislavgrad. We saw earlier where Topic is saying that electricity can go to Croatia. You actually gave us an explanation, but perhaps you can give us a very brief explanation as to what is happening in this particular document, assuming you have the necessary background and information to do so.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I would just like to explain it briefly. When you build a hydro-electric power-plant, that usually implies artificial lake and that artificial lake would then flood or submerge a certain area in the ex-state, and today the municipality where the land is submerged are compensated for that. So in this case the plant is in the Republic of Croatia, while the accumulation, artificial lake, or the reservoir is in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the municipality of Livno, and submerges areas of the Livno and Tomislavgrad municipalities. Of course, for this there has to be compensation. I don't want to go into the amounts, but there is a right to compensation pursuant to some sort of regulation or agreement or some kind of deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, did this particular arrangement exist prior to the war? Are you aware of this particular situation, that is, in Tomislavgrad and Busko Lake dam? Would this exist prior to the war or was this something that was built during the war?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: It was before the war. This is just a continuation of the activity from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does it continue on today?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would I take it that even today there has to be some sort of compensation, similar to what we see in this document?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, there is a duty and there are different agreements also about how to resolve this issue. Now, there is probably a specific agreement about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 01805, this is a payroll sheet. Again, we don't have to busy ourselves too much about this, but the date is rather important, December 1992. Do you recognise the list -- well, first, do you recognise this power company, EPHZ?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And am I correct that number 2, Zulfo Robovic, and number 4, Edin Omeragic, are Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, they're Muslims and the entire team is actually the management team of the enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we go to 1D 01806, this is dated 11 January 1993, again the date is rather significant for us. And we see that this is -- these are minutes of a session of a management board. The document is signed by the president, Azer Sirko, the secretary is Djula Hasanagic, I think I got the name right. First of all, are you familiar with this company, Elektroprivreda?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I know the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how important is this company, especially in light of the time, 11 January 1993, what does it actually do?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: The company is exceptionally important. It supplies the area with electricity, both citizens and companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, it says here at some point by the decision -- "by its decision, the founder appointed Azer Sirko president of the board and Blago Planinic vice-president" and of course later on we see that at the proposal of the acting director general, Djula Hasanagic, was unanimously elected secretary of the management board. If you could please tell us whether these are important positions.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Mr. Azer Sirko here is the president of the board of directors. This is the highest position of that company. The secretary of the board is Djuko Hasanagic. And the other -- well, this is one position and the other one is the position of treasurer and both of those positions are very important in the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And are they not Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: They are Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at the next document 1D 01807, and this is -- we see this is minutes, extracts from a meeting, and it says that: "... on the 17th of March, 1993," again I point that out for the benefit of all, "the management board" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas, to interrupt you. I have only a question which is really not in a way controversial I hope. Since the -- one of the persons mentioned before Djula Hasanagic, I believe, since Djula is a Hungarian first name, I wonder if the witness knows if he was Muslim with a Muslim name but in a way partly or mainly Hungarian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sure that this is a Muslim -- a Muslim woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: All right. Then I give it up, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 01807, we see that at a meeting of 17th March 1993, the management board of Elektroprivreda discussed the extremely serious electrical power situation in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if we go -- I don't want to -- if we go to the third paragraph and it says here: "The promises made and measures taken by the Ministry of Energy and Electric Power Industry of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that production would restart within the set dead-line were not fulfilled, and without energy production there were bound to be serious problems with the system." Could you please explain what Mr. Sirko is saying here.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: At that time the system was in jeopardy because there were no stable sources of electricity that were working. They were either not working or they were not linked to the system, and the stable electricity sources were thermo-electric power-plants. So the system now depended on the hydro-electric power-plants which in turn depended on the rain, on precipitation. This year was a year of very little snow, so there wasn't enough water in the reservoirs in order to fill their capacity so it was a problem, how to secure electricity for Bosnia and Herzegovina and for our region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at paragraph number 6, maybe you could help us out here in light of your previous testimony. It says: "The HZ HB Elektroprivreda, JP," shall -- "will insist on the implementation of the conclusions from the meeting of 23 February 1993 on the delivery of electricity to Sarajevo and Central Bosnia, the quantity as agreed with the HEP, Croatian Electricity Supply Board, and the Bosnia and Herzegovina EP." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that point in time, it would appear that some sort of an agreement was made to deliver electricity to Sarajevo and Central Bosnia. Was it possible, in light of the circumstances, we're talking on or about 17 March 1993, the discussion having taken place on 23 February 1993, what exactly are they talking about?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: There was a shortage of electricity in the area where this public electrical supply in Bosnia was operating. So the electrical supply industry of the Republic of Croatia, Republic of Bosnia, and from Herceg-Bosna, needed to see how to resolve this issue. So what they thought was to get the electricity from the Republic of Croatia in order to resolve these problems, and the electrical supply industry from Bosnia insisted that these negotiations be finalised -- actually, what it says here is that they would insist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The industry from Bosnia-Herzegovina or Herceg-Bosna, which of the ... it says here that --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I was not talking -- saying anything about the industry, I wasn't talking about industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But it says here in your answer that: "So what they thought was to get the electricity from the Republic of Croatia in order to resolve these problems and the electricity supply industry from Bosnia insisted on these negotiations being finalised ..." are we talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina or are we talking about Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I think that the interpretation is wrong. Perhaps I spoke too fast. From what I understood, agreement was reached to resolve problems of the shortage of the electricity power-supply in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was also a shortage in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, there were problems in Central Bosnia, and there were problems in the supply of Sarajevo with electricity. And at the time they tried to resolve this in cooperation with the Republic of Croatia with the electric power-supply companies of the Republic of Croatia so that the power from the Republic of Croatia to Central Bosnia and Sarajevo was supposed to be transmitted by the power transmission lines through Herceg-Bosna so that the Elektroprivreda of Herceg-Bosna was going to insist that those negotiations would be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And were they completed to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. The situation kept improving. Only during conflict or clashes or combat the situation would deteriorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe this may be the time for the break or do I continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing's resumed. You may proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I understand I have 31 minutes left, 31. We will try to do it in 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, if you could -- we're going to go to the next -- next topic which deals with PTT matters. We're going to skip one document, so I'm -- the one -- so skip one document and look at 1D 02671, 1D 02671. This is dated 17 May 1992, as you will see, and the reason I'm skipping is to save a little time. If we look at the end of the document we see that this is by Enes Santic who is the president of the Crisis Staff of PTT. Of course we noted the date, and here this is a report on the state of the postal, telephone, and telecommunications facilities. I'm not going to go through this, but I do want to focus your attention on paragraph number 5 where it says: "The following persons are engaged in the aforementioned tasks and they are giving us their assistance, Mr. Ilija Kozulj, graduate engineer; Mr. Mario Orec, graduated engineer, employees of UNIS system." And as I understand it that at that point in time you were with the special-purpose council, is that correct, from the earlier documents that we saw?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did you know Mr. Santic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I know Mr. Santic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document, 1D 00906, and here it says the subject is providing for an unobstructed PTT communication connection in the territory, or the area I believe it says in the original version - I don't want to go into that whole discussion, Your Honours - but as I understand the original version is area of Herceg-Bosna, and we see Grude, Ljubuski, Capljina, Neum, Citluk, Siroki Brijeg, Posusje, Livno, and Tomislavgrad, and of course this is by -- for the HVO chief coordinator of the PTT service Mladen Zulj. And I guess if you could help us out, in this area and the lists of these various municipalities, one, we don't see Mostar; and two, can you account why these particular municipalities, is there some significance that Mr. Zulj has asked for an unobstructed PTT communications system there?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: First of all, these are municipalities that at the time were free, liberated. We need to add Mostar here as well, which was partially free, but the telephone exchange in Mostar was completely destroyed at the time so there was nothing to reduce. He's asking here that telephone lines -- the use of telephone lines be reduced and that communication among the centres is secured to put priorities on essential needs in wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document, 1D 00602, this is 24 July 1992, and this is on the installation and use of telephones in the Mostar municipality. Do you know why this decision was necessary?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: At the time there were no telephones in Mostar, at the time we went back some 40 years and so we had a hand-operated telephone exchange that we used for communication. It was necessary to set up a kind of rule book whom to provide telephone lines to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Next, 3D 00658, this is dated 10 August 1992, this is to Mostar PTT. And this is to: "Please provide us with three lines to connect the following routes ..." And it's by Arif Pasalic. Did you know Mr. Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all extra microphones be switched off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, I do know Mr. Arif Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you know why he was asking for these three lines, do you know these locations?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I am familiar with these locations. He wanted lines to be secured for internal needs. These are not telephone connections but lines that are used for internal communications between these points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just for your information, we haven't got this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm shocked. 3D 00658. I'll see to it -- we can put it right on the ELMO right now. It's an exhibit, it's in the e-court, this is complements of the Praljak team --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But it should have been -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document 1D 00063, we have here a decision to establish a public enterprise for postal and telecommunications service in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna during - and I underscore that word - during a state of imminent threat of war. Have you had a chance to look at this document, sir, and could you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why would this be necessary? Why -- why is it necessary to pass this decision?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: It was necessary to merge all the parts of enterprises that were in this field so that we could secure communications for the needs of the defence, for the needs of the businesses, the needs of the citizens. We're talking about parts of the PTT companies in Mostar as well as other companies on the free territory of -- in Bosnia and in Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document, 1D 02670, this is a report on the possibilities for improving the system of telecommunications. Are you familiar with this document, sir; and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: A public company was formed in Mostar for the construction and rebuilding of Mostar, and that dealt with the rebuilding of the infrastructure and public companies. We organized a counselling session or advisory session at the headquarters of that company and we tried to get as many people as possible to see how we could restore and rebuild the communications system in the territory that - how can I put it? - we had under our control. So that was a part of the group that was at that meeting. The objective was to agree on how to resolve technical issues in the best possible way. One of the solutions was given as -- or from a third party -- on page 3 on how to deal with this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, we'll get to that. But first: Who prepared this report? I know you told us why it was prepared and the involvement of the -- this public company for reconstruction and rebuilding, but the text of this report?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I prepared it or drafted it personally for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And do you recall about what period of time?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Summer 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the last page, it would be the last page for everyone, we see this schematic. Maybe we can put one of them on the ELMO and maybe you can explain to us on the ELMO, you can point how to read this schematic. First, if I could ask you, who prepared this schematic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: UNIS Telekom Mostar and its teams provided assistance to the PTT in repairing the telecommunications system. They made available material, equipment, and personnel, and they had a team that made designs for various technical solutions, various projects. And this is one such plan or design that was, for the most part, implemented. This was done by Armin Kulundzija and I have to tell you that he is a Muslim because that's what you always ask me, he worked in Mostar. And now since Mostar -- at this time, before it was destroyed, it had a link with Sarajevo and this is not drawn in here because this line was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: It was also linked up --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We have to go step by step. And first if you could look to your right.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it might be good if you want to either point or you can even mark and go step by step. Some of us may not be able to understand this, and I can assure you that I'm one of those folks. So can you walk us through this schematic.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can. So this is Mostar, and there was a coaxial cable laid down linking it with Sarajevo; and this line was disrupted, it is not depicted here. Secondly, there was a relay station located in the area controlled by the Serb army at the time, Paric, that was its name, and Mostar was linked through this relay station with Titograd and the same relay station was used to link Mostar with Split. Now, since the relay station was captured we didn't know what was going on. It was not destroyed but it was just captured and all the equipment there was switched off. So all those large systems that were the basis for the communications system linking Mostar with the broader area were destroyed. And now this solution calls for a building of a completely new relay station on a hill near Mostar, to build a facility there, a building, to lay power lines to that area, to build up a tower, to set up aerials. Now, I don't need to go into details here, but it is important to note that this would make it possible to re-establish communication lines with Split and also to establish communication lines throughout Herzegovina. But at the same time, it would be possible through these points Plejin Vrh and Cvrsnica, Plocno, to establish communication lines with Central Bosnia. So this solution envisages a link from Plocno to Sarajevo. So at that time we were trying to figure out how we could link up Sarajevo with this whole network, thereby making up for what was lost and what existed before the war. This plan was not implemented fully. We improved it even better and we got even closer to Sarajevo, just a few steps away from Sarajevo. So the initial idea was from Cvrsnica to Bjelasnica and then you had to go from Bjelasnica to Sarajevo and at that time Bjelasnica was under threat. I don't know whether it was perhaps destroyed at that time, but we were able to come really close to Sarajevo and it was all in place, it was all implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Just two things if you could do. If you could take a pen and just draw where this coaxial cable would have been located and where it was -- you indicated that it was cut. If you could just draw that on there.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: It was cut in several places, at the so-called Carinski Most, the customs bridge in Mostar crossing over to the left bank, and then at the railway bridge north of the town. So two bridges were destroyed and cables were laid on those bridges including the one leading to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very good. And then if you could tell us where -- draw where the relay station would have been, in which direction, because you mentioned a relay station that would have connected with, I believe, Split.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: This relay station -- so first of all the communication line went from Mostar to this relay station, and then from there to Titograd, and another communications station to Plejin Vrh and then on to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you've been saying Titograd and some of us may know where that is --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Podgorica, that's -- Podgorica today. That's its name today. It's the capital of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Exactly. Thank you. If we go on to the next chapter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just an additional question, Witness. You have said that the coaxial cable was interrupted at two points --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least at two places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. Were there no damages, no interruptions, do you know anything about this between the immediate surroundings of Mostar and Sarajevo? I suppose that the line passed through Serb-controlled areas. Do you know whether it was also cut there? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This cable passed through the Serb-controlled area up until the closest vicinity of Sarajevo. I don't know where it was cut. I don't know whether there were any major bridges there, but I know for sure about the disruptions or -- in Mostar. The two bridges, the customs bridge and the railway bridge, they were destroyed and that's why the cables were cut at those places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question, it's not technical but it has to do with this report we have, 1D 2670. I note that UNIS Telekom is quite a large company, it's supposed to do all the work for this -- for these telephone lines and it dates back to 1979. In this document it seems that UNIS Telekom has a long-term contract with a Swedish company called Ericsson. This is what is written in this document. In this document it seems that UNIS Telekom is going to have a role to play to put all these lines up again and therefore there is a description, and I don't have much to say about this, but this is what I note, it seems that Ericsson is going to be set aside because on the paragraph before last it seems that UNIS is going to do this work with partners from Croatia. So can you tell me exactly what happened? Why is it that Ericsson suddenly disappears from the scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Ericsson did not disappear, Your Honour. Ericsson remained the partner of UNIS Telekom but please bear in mind that the public company that was post and telecommunications, it's a public company, whereas UNIS Telekom is a state or socially owned company and it is a normal business operating in accordance with the laws of economics. During the war whatever UNIS Telekom did for post or telecommunications or anyone else, it submitted a bill and it collected the money, perhaps not immediately. But as soon as it became possible to collect the money for the services delivered, it did so. If necessary, it could contract out anything. It could work with Siemens or with Ericsson, because you have to know that Ericsson has a similar production plant in Zagreb. There is a Nikola Tesla factory which is owned by Ericsson now, and at that time it was based on the same principle as the UNIS Telekom. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll go on to the next segment very quickly. This deals with the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm told that I need to ask for an IC number with the document that we had on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the diagram shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00848. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 02038, this is a decision on the election of the president, vice-president, members of the government, and we see that your name is there as minister of transport and communication. This is what you were telling us earlier, that you were appointed as minister of the Croatian Republic -- as one of the ministers in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; correct.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we can see the date is 20 November 1993. If we look at the next document, 1D 01982, this is signed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic, president of the government of Herceg-Bosna, that's how -- what it says in English. It's the subject matter, meeting between the representatives of the Government of the Republic of Croatia and the Government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna for economic issues ... and we see it's 14 December 1993. It then talks about an agreement of 19 November and 3 December 1993, the meetings between the delegation of the Government of the Republic of Croatia and the Government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and then it -- then we see that certain recommendations are being made, one of them is: "Cooperation in the field of public enterprises, electricity supplies, the railroad, water-supply, post and telecommunications, roads." And then we see that the meeting will be attended and the minister of transport and communications is going to be one of the individuals participating in the meeting. If you could tell us very briefly, what was this meeting about, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I do recall. At that time we had a meeting where we discussed how the cooperation in the areas of infrastructure and economy could be improved between the two governments. So this is the topic of our discussion. A number of issues came up and we tried to deal with them to find solutions -- well, I don't want to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's sufficient. Now, before I show you the next document, which is 1D 01977, if you could briefly tell us how is it that you were appointed to the position of minister of transport and communications? If you could be very brief about it.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I was in Zagreb at the time on a trip that had to do with some family issues, and as I was watching TV I saw that I was appointed a minister in the Government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I called Mr. Prlic and I asked him what this was all about. And he told me, I was asked to put in a recommendation and I recommended you and this is now done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- and did there come a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This is rather surprising. Are you saying that you were elected by surprise for yourself? You learned on television?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He was nominated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Or you were nominated. Was that a full surprise, as you seem to have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it came as a surprise for me and I have to say that it was also an honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, maybe I should have asked another question as well on top of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How many individuals were there at that time in and around the location with your sort of background and experience?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, a limited number of people, people who had expertise and some ability were few and far between, but -- and I also have to say that in the area that I dealt with I don't know anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And now -- did -- what made you actually accept the position? I know that you were informed, Mr. Prlic said he put your name on the list, that's the way it is. Did there come a time when you had to make a decision whether you would actually accept the position if indeed elected to it; and if so, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that I was encouraged by the first session of the Government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the president also participated, Mr. Mate Boban; and at that meeting a number of issues and tasks were discussed, issues and tasks of the government. And one of the major issues was that the government would make sure that law and order were imposed and that international conventions would be complied with in every way. And for me this was an impetus for me to get really involved in the work of this government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at 1D 01977 now, and this is a report dated 27 December 1993, keeping in mind your particular work that you were involved with, are you familiar with the contents of this report and can you tell us to any degree of certainty whether this report comports with efforts that were being made as described in this report as at the time?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of it at the time and I knew about the contents of this document, and it is in line with what was agreed at the first session of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document, P 07825, this is titled declaration. If we look at the last page we see this is 8 February 1994, Livno. Were you in Livno by any chance?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Livno at the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were you there when this declaration was drafted?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I'm not going to go into it with any detail, but let's look at the next document, 1D 01614. And this is 9 February 1994, these are the minutes of the 14th Session. We see that you're there, and if we go -- without going through the document in any degree of detail, if we look at item 16 which would be on the last page in the English version, page 5, Your Honours, it says: "In the statement from today's session of the government points out that the Government will do its part in keeping with the adopted declaration from the extraordinary session of the House of Representatives of the Assembly of the HR HB in Livno." Looking at this part, the declaration that they're referring to here, that's the declaration that we just saw; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you know -- now going back to the declaration for one second, can you tell us what this declaration was about? What was the purpose for having this declaration?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I see this declaration as follows. First of all, in terms of the text of this declaration, I find it acceptable and I found it acceptable at the time. It was adopted at the time when it seemed that peace was in our -- within our grasp because there were firm agreements in place that Bosnia and Herzegovina would establish as a state consisting of three republics, and we in Livno were happy that the time had come for the war to stop and to start the reconstruction and re-establishment of normal life in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the union of three republics, that peace agreement you're referring to is the Owen-Stoltenberg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just have a couple more documents left and then I'll be through. The next segment deals with the Washington --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The last document -- the last segment which deals with the Washington Agreement, if we look at 1D 01953, we see it's -- at the top we see 23 April 1994. We see your name here. These are notes from a meeting of the representatives of the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna held on 6th April, and of course it's in the context of the implementation of the Washington Agreement. And then of course if we look at paragraphs number 4, number 7, they deal with sort of areas you've discussed. Do you know what this document is about and were you -- can you tell us a little bit about the meeting? Let me put it that way, and we see by the way Mr. Faruk Sma ilbegovic.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, it was a meeting in Mr. Jadranko Prlic's office. That was the first meeting I had with the officials from Sarajevo. There were two of my friends in that delegation, Faruk Smailbegovic and Ibro Koludar and there was a long debate at this meeting about various issues in an effort to establish contacts and to start work, start cooperation, on various issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And did that -- was it a successful meeting?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: In my opinion, it was, particularly because other meetings followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 02668, this is a report on the implementation of the Washington Agreement and the Constitution of the Federation of BH. If we look at it, it lists various dates in the first page and the introduction, and then we see contents about roads, railway, post and telecommunications, radio, television, and so on. Can you please tell us if you recognise this document; and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: I do recognise this document; I drafted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know about when? I know that the last date that we see is 31st August 1994, and can you tell us about when?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, it was sometime in September that year or perhaps -- well, September or October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And finally the last document, 1D 02672, it says here: "Postal services and telecommunications in Mostar area in the period of homeland war. "Remarks." If we look at the end of this document it's Mostar, 30th of June, 2007. Can you please tell us if you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How is it that you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, when I was told that -- well, first of all, I drafted it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: So when I was told that I should come here and testify before this Tribunal, I went through the documents that I had in my personal files from that period and I put together a kind of a summary of the relevant activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in fact, if I may lead you, during the proofing session yesterday you pointed it out to me that this was a document that you had prepared; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I have just one last final question. If you could please describe to the Trial Chamber your first visit to Sarajevo after you were appointed to your position, your first visit to Sarajevo, what transpired. And in that, if you could please give us a few words about Dr. Jadranko Prlic and his efforts during that first visit as well and his efforts thereafter.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: First of all, after this first meeting we arranged -- we decided that such a visit should be arranged and a large group of people from Mostar headed to Sarajevo. I was in that team and so were my associates. When we got close to Sarajevo, we were told that we could not cross -- we could not go across the airport to get into Sarajevo, we had to use the tunnel. It was a make-shift tunnel that was used to go in and out of Sarajevo, and that's what we did. It was very difficult, almost impossible, but we got in and we held those talks. I was quite happy with the outcome of the talks. There were quite a few initiatives that were tabled on our side, and I think that those initiatives were accepted at those meetings; but unfortunately it seemed that at some place they were blocked. That was my impression. As far as I was concerned, I told Mr. Prlic that I did not want to pass the tunnel, I couldn't pass through it anymore, and I know that he passed through it dozens of times. And I know that he put in a lot of effort to establish a good joint government; that's what I know. Well, we're running out of time so I can't go into any more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The last question is: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Well, there is a date here. It was I think the 29th of April, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, it was three days, from the 27th until the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: April 19 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ
utterances.text: 27th until the 29th April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kozulj. I have no further questions. I really appreciate you answering all the questions that anyone else may pose to you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have 15 minutes left. Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. You'll be glad to learn that the Defence for Bruno Stojic have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
